course.title: C Programming from Zero to Hero
course.description: Learn C from scratch: setup, variables, loops, functions, pointers, structures and files, ending with a mini project that manages student marks.

lessons.title: C Setup & Your First Program
lessons.body:
What is C?

C is a fast, general-purpose programming language created in the 1970s. Operating systems, embedded devices and many other languages are built with C. Learning C teaches you how a computer really works: memory, variables and the CPU.

Step 1: Install a compiler

C code must be compiled (translated to machine code) before it runs. Install GCC: on Windows use MinGW, on macOS run xcode-select --install, on Linux run sudo apt install gcc. Check it with gcc --version.

Step 2: Write your first program

Save this as hello.c:

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    printf("Hello, World!\n");
    return 0;
}

Step 3: Compile and run

Compile with gcc hello.c -o hello, then run it with ./hello on Linux/macOS or hello.exe on Windows. You should see Hello, World!.

How the program works: #include <stdio.h> brings in the standard input/output library so we can use printf. Every C program starts at main. printf prints text, and \n is a newline. return 0; tells the operating system the program finished successfully. Every statement ends with a semicolon.

Key points

  • C code must be compiled with a compiler such as GCC before it can run.
  • Every C program starts execution in the main function.
  • #include <stdio.h> gives you printf for printing output.
  • Every statement ends with a semicolon, and return 0; means success.
  • Compile with gcc hello.c -o hello and run the result.

mcqs.q: Which function is the entry point of every C program?
mcqs.why: Execution of every C program begins in the main() function; the other names have no special meaning.

mcqs.q: Which header file must be included to use printf()?
mcqs.why: printf() is declared in stdio.h, the standard input/output header.

mcqs.q: Which command compiles hello.c into a program called hello?
mcqs.why: gcc is the compiler; -o hello names the output executable file.

mcqs.q: What does return 0; in main() mean?
mcqs.why: By convention, returning 0 from main() signals successful completion to the operating system.

mcqs.q: Which is a valid C source file name?
mcqs.why: C source files use the .c extension; the others belong to C++, Python and Java.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.expected: Hello, World!
tasks.answer: printf prints the text exactly as written, and \n moves to a new line.
tasks.hint: printf prints the string literally; \n is just a newline.

tasks.title: Fix the missing semicolon
tasks.prompt: This program will not compile. Find and fix the bug.
tasks.answer: The printf statement is missing its semicolon. In C every statement must end with ;, so the compiler reports an error before the return statement.
tasks.hint: Every statement in C ends with a specific character. Which line is missing it?

tasks.title: Fill in the blanks
tasks.prompt: Complete the program so it prints your name.
tasks.expected:
#include
return
tasks.answer: #include brings in stdio.h so printf works, and return 0; ends main() with success.
tasks.hint: The first blank is the preprocessor directive; the second blank is the keyword that hands 0 back.

lessons.title: Variables, Data Types & Input/Output
lessons.body:
Variables: named boxes in memory

A variable is a named place in memory that stores a value. You declare it with a type and a name, then you can store and change values in it: int age = 21;

The main data types

  • int — whole numbers, e.g. 42, -7
  • float — decimal numbers, e.g. 3.14 (use double for more precision)
  • char — a single character in single quotes, e.g. 'A'

Printing with printf

Format specifiers tell printf what type to print: %d for int, %f for float/double, %c for char. Using the wrong specifier prints garbage.

Reading input with scanf

scanf reads typed input. It needs the address of the variable, so you write & before the variable name: scanf("%d", &age);. Forgetting the & is the most common beginner crash.

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int age;
    float height;
    printf("Enter your age: ");
    scanf("%d", &age);
    printf("Enter your height in metres: ");
    scanf("%f", &height);
    printf("Age: %d, Height: %.2f\n", age, height);
    return 0;
}

%.2f prints a float with 2 digits after the decimal point. Always initialise your variables — an uninitialised variable holds whatever garbage was already in that memory.

Key points

  • Declare a variable with a type: int, float, double or char.
  • Use matching format specifiers: %d for int, %f for float, %c for char.
  • scanf needs the address of the variable: scanf("%d", &age);
  • Always initialise variables; uninitialised variables hold garbage values.
  • %.2f prints a float rounded to 2 decimal places.

mcqs.q: Which format specifier prints a float?
mcqs.why: %f is the specifier for float (and double) values; %d is for int, %c for char, %s for strings.

mcqs.q: What is missing in this line? scanf("%d", age);
mcqs.why: scanf needs the address of the variable, so it must be scanf("%d", &age); — without & it writes to a wrong address.

mcqs.q: What value does an uninitialised local int variable hold?
mcqs.why: C does not zero local variables automatically; the memory holds whatever was there before, so the value is unpredictable.

mcqs.q: Which is a valid variable name in C?
mcqs.why: Names must start with a letter or underscore and contain only letters, digits and underscores; int is a reserved keyword and 2marks starts with a digit.

mcqs.q: What does printf("%.2f", 3.14159); print?
mcqs.why: %.2f rounds the float to exactly 2 digits after the decimal point.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: %d prints the int 5, %.1f prints the float 2.5 rounded to one decimal place.
tasks.hint: Match each specifier to its value: %d with 5, %.1f with 2.5.

tasks.title: Fix the scanf crash
tasks.prompt: This program crashes when run. Find and fix the bug.
tasks.answer: scanf needs the address of marks so it knows where to store the input. Without &, scanf treats the garbage value of marks as an address and writes to random memory, which crashes the program.
tasks.hint: scanf stores input somewhere — what does it need to know where?

tasks.title: Fill in the blanks
tasks.prompt: Complete the program so it reads a number and prints it back doubled.
tasks.answer: scanf needs &n to store the input, and n * 2 doubles the value.
tasks.hint: First blank: scanf needs an address. Second blank: what number doubles n?

lessons.title: Operators & If-Else Decisions
lessons.body:
Operators

Operators act on values: arithmetic (+ - * / %), relational (== != < > <= >=) and logical (&& AND, || OR, ! NOT). The remainder operator % gives what is left after division: 7 % 3 is 1.

The integer division trap

Dividing two ints gives an int — the fraction is thrown away, not rounded. 5 / 2 is 2, not 2.5. To get 2.5, make one side a float: 5 / 2.0.

Making decisions with if-else

An if runs its block only when its condition is true. else if chains extra checks, and else catches everything else. The condition uses == for comparison — a single = assigns a value instead of comparing, which is a classic bug.

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int marks;
    printf("Enter marks: ");
    scanf("%d", &marks);
    if (marks >= 90) {
        printf("Grade A\n");
    } else if (marks >= 40) {
        printf("Pass\n");
    } else {
        printf("Fail\n");
    }
    return 0;
}

Trace it: marks 95 hits the first branch and skips the rest; marks 60 fails the first test, passes the second and prints Pass; marks 20 prints Fail.

Key points

  • 5 / 2 is 2 in C because int divided by int gives an int.
  • % gives the remainder: 7 % 3 is 1.
  • Use == to compare and = to assign — never mix them up.
  • if / else if / else runs exactly one branch, the first whose condition is true.
  • Combine conditions with && (AND) and || (OR).

flowchart.title: How an if-else decides pass or fail

mcqs.q: What is the value of 5 / 2 in C?
mcqs.why: Both operands are ints, so C performs integer division and discards the fraction: 5 / 2 is 2.

mcqs.q: What is 7 % 3 in C?
mcqs.why: 7 divided by 3 is 2 remainder 1, and % returns that remainder.

mcqs.q: What is wrong with if (marks = 40)?
options: It assigns 40 to marks instead of comparing
mcqs.why: A single = assigns 40 to marks (and the condition becomes 40, which is true); comparison needs ==.

mcqs.q: In if (a > 0 && b > 0), when is the condition true?
options: When both a and b are positive
When a and b are equal
When either a or b is positive
mcqs.why: && is logical AND, so the whole condition is true only when both sides are true.

mcqs.q: marks is 35. What does the lesson program print?
mcqs.why: 35 is below 90 and below 40, so both if tests fail and the else branch prints Fail.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: a / b is integer division, 5 / 2 = 2, and a % b is the remainder, 5 % 2 = 1.
tasks.hint: Remember: int / int drops the fraction, and % gives the remainder.

tasks.title: Fix the comparison bug
tasks.prompt: This program always prints 'Equal' even for different numbers. Fix it.
tasks.answer: a = b assigns 9 to a, and the condition then tests 9, which is non-zero and therefore true. Changing = to == compares the values, so 5 == 9 is false and it prints 'Not equal'.
tasks.hint: One character is the difference between assigning and comparing.

tasks.title: Trace the if-else chain
tasks.prompt: Trace the lesson program step by step when marks is 60.
tasks.expected: marks=60; 60>=90 is false; 60>=40 is true; prints Pass; else skipped.
tasks.answer: Following the flowchart: the first decision (marks >= 90?) is No, so control moves to the second decision (marks >= 40?), which is Yes, so it prints Pass and skips the else branch entirely.
tasks.hint: Walk the flowchart: check each decision in order and take the Yes/No edge.

lessons.title: Loops: for, while & do-while
lessons.body:
Why loops?

A loop repeats a block of code instead of you writing it again and again. C has three loops: for, while and do-while.

The for loop

Use for when you know how many times to repeat. It packs start, condition and step into one line: for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) runs with i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

The while loop

while checks its condition before each run, so it may run zero times. It suits loops where the number of repeats is unknown, like reading input until the user types 0.

The do-while loop

do-while checks its condition after each run, so the body always runs at least once — perfect for menus that must show once before asking.

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int i, sum = 0;
    for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
        sum = sum + i;
    }
    printf("Sum 1 to 5 = %d\n", sum);
    return 0;
}

Trace: i=1 sum=1, i=2 sum=3, i=3 sum=6, i=4 sum=10, i=5 sum=15, then i becomes 6, the condition fails and the loop ends. break exits a loop early and continue skips to the next round. Forgetting to update the loop variable inside a while creates an infinite loop.

Key points

  • for is best when the number of repeats is known.
  • while checks the condition before each run and may run zero times.
  • do-while always runs the body at least once.
  • break exits a loop; continue skips to the next iteration.
  • Always update the loop variable, or a while loop runs forever.

flowchart.title: How a for loop adds 1 to 5

mcqs.q: What does the lesson program print?
mcqs.why: 1+2+3+4+5 = 15, so sum is 15 when the loop ends.

mcqs.q: Which loop always runs its body at least once?
mcqs.why: do-while tests its condition after the body, so the first run happens unconditionally.

mcqs.q: What does break do inside a loop?
mcqs.why: break jumps out of the loop at once; continue is the one that skips to the next iteration.

mcqs.q: How many times does for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) run its body?
mcqs.why: i takes the values 0, 1 and 2 — three runs — and stops when i becomes 3.

mcqs.q: What happens if a while loop never changes its condition variable?
mcqs.why: The condition stays true, so the loop never exits — an infinite loop.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: i runs 1, 2, 3 and i*i gives 1, 4, 9, each followed by a space.
tasks.hint: The loop prints i squared for i = 1, 2, 3.

tasks.title: Fix the infinite loop
tasks.prompt: This while loop never ends. Fix it so it prints 1 to 5.
tasks.answer: i is never updated inside the loop, so i <= 5 stays true forever. Adding i++ makes i grow until the condition fails and the loop ends after printing 1 to 5.
tasks.hint: Something inside the loop body must move i towards the exit condition.

tasks.title: Fill in the blanks
tasks.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints the numbers 10 down to 1.
tasks.answer: The loop must stop at 1, so the condition is i >= 1, and i-- counts down by one each round.
tasks.hint: First blank: the last number to print. Second blank: how do you count down?

lessons.title: Functions & Scope
lessons.body:
Why functions?

A function is a named block of code that does one job. Instead of copying the same code everywhere, you write it once and call it: add(3, 4). Functions make programs shorter, clearer and easier to debug.

Anatomy of a function

A function has a return type, a name, parameters (inputs) and a body. int add(int a, int b) takes two ints and returns an int. A function that returns nothing uses void.

Declare before you use

C must see a function before it is called. Either define the function above main, or put a prototype (declaration) above main and define it below.

Scope: local vs global

A variable declared inside a function is local — it exists only there and disappears when the function returns. A variable declared outside all functions is global and visible everywhere, but globals should be used sparingly because any function can change them.

#include <stdio.h>

int add(int a, int b)
{
    return a + b;
}

int main(void)
{
    int result = add(3, 4);
    printf("3 + 4 = %d\n", result);
    return 0;
}

Flow: main calls add(3, 4), control jumps into add, a + b is 7, return sends 7 back, and main stores it in result. Arguments are copied into parameters, so changing a parameter inside the function never changes the caller's variable.

Key points

  • A function groups one job into a reusable, named block of code.
  • The return type says what the function gives back; void means nothing.
  • Declare a function (or its prototype) before calling it.
  • Local variables exist only inside their function; globals are visible everywhere.
  • Arguments are copied into parameters, so the caller's variables are unchanged.

mcqs.q: What does int add(int a, int b) return?
mcqs.why: The return type int before the name means the function returns one int value.

mcqs.q: What does void mean as a function return type?
mcqs.why: void means the function returns no value at all.

mcqs.q: Where is a local variable visible?
options: Only inside the function where it is declared
mcqs.why: Local variables are scoped to the block they are declared in and cease to exist when the function returns.

mcqs.q: What happens if you call a function that has not been declared yet?
mcqs.why: C needs to see a declaration or prototype before a call, otherwise the compiler does not know the function's signature.

mcqs.q: What does add(3, 4) return in the lesson program?
mcqs.why: add returns a + b, and 3 + 4 is 7.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: square(6) returns 6 * 6 = 36, and main prints that value.
tasks.hint: Follow the call: 6 goes into n, and the function returns n * n.

tasks.title: Fix the missing declaration
tasks.prompt: This program fails to compile. Fix it with the smallest change.
tasks.answer: main calls double_it before the compiler has seen it. Adding the prototype int double_it(int n); above main tells the compiler the signature, so the call compiles and the definition below main still provides the body.
tasks.hint: C must know a function exists before it is called — how do you announce it early?

tasks.title: Trace the function call
tasks.prompt: Trace this program step by step.
tasks.expected: main calls add(3,4); a=3, b=4 inside add; returns 7; result=7; prints 7.
tasks.answer: Following the flowchart: main calls add, the arguments are copied into a and b, add returns 7, control returns to main, result becomes 7 and printf prints 7.
tasks.hint: Walk the flowchart: call, copy arguments, compute, return, print.

lessons.title: Arrays & Strings
lessons.body:
Arrays: many values, one name

An array stores many values of the same type under one name: int marks[5] = {78, 85, 90, 66, 92}; holds five marks. Indexing starts at 0, so the first mark is marks[0] and the last is marks[4].

Stay inside the bounds

C does not check array bounds. Reading or writing marks[5] in a 5-element array touches memory that is not yours — undefined behaviour, often a crash or corrupted data. Always loop from 0 to size - 1.

Strings are char arrays

A string is a char array ending with the null character '\\0', which marks the end. char name[20] = "Sid"; stores 'S', 'i', 'd', '\\0'. Print strings with %s and read a word with scanf("%19s", name) — no & needed because the array name is already an address.

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int marks[5] = {78, 85, 90, 66, 92};
    int i, sum = 0;
    for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        sum = sum + marks[i];
    }
    printf("Total: %d, Average: %.1f\n", sum, sum / 5.0);
    char name[20] = "Sid";
    printf("Hello, %s\n", name);
    return 0;
}

Note sum / 5.0: dividing by 5.0 forces floating-point division, so the average is 82.2 instead of the truncated int result 82.

Key points

  • Arrays hold many values of one type; indexing starts at 0.
  • A 5-element array has valid indices 0 to 4 — never read arr[5].
  • A string is a char array ending with the null character '\\0'.
  • Print strings with %s; scanf("%s") needs no & for arrays.
  • Use sum / 5.0 (not sum / 5) to get a real average.

mcqs.q: What is the first element of int arr[5]?
mcqs.why: C arrays are zero-indexed, so the first element is arr[0].

mcqs.q: What happens if you read arr[5] in a 5-element array?
options: Undefined behaviour — memory outside the array
mcqs.why: C does no bounds checking, so arr[5] reads memory past the array; the result is undefined and can crash or corrupt data.

mcqs.q: What marks the end of a C string?
mcqs.why: C strings are char arrays terminated by '\0'; functions like printf("%s") stop there.

mcqs.q: How many elements are in int a[10]?
mcqs.why: The size in brackets is the element count: a[10] holds 10 elements, indices 0 to 9.

mcqs.q: int marks[5] = {78, 85, 90, 66, 92}; What is the total?

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: a[0] is the first element 10 and a[3] is the last element 40.
tasks.hint: Count from 0: the first element is index 0, the fourth is index 3.

tasks.title: Fix the out-of-bounds loop
tasks.prompt: This loop reads past the end of the array. Fix it.
tasks.answer: i <= 5 lets i reach 5, and a[5] is outside the 5-element array (valid indices 0-4). Changing the condition to i < 5 keeps every access inside the array.
tasks.hint: For an array of size 5, what is the largest safe index?

tasks.title: Fill in the blanks
tasks.prompt: Complete the program so it prints the name stored in the string.
tasks.expected:
Sid
%s
tasks.answer: The string is initialised to "Sid" and %s is the format specifier that prints a string.
tasks.hint: First blank: any name in quotes. Second blank: the specifier for a string.

lessons.title: Pointers & Memory
lessons.body:
What is a pointer?

A pointer is a variable that stores a memory address instead of a value. It lets a function change the caller's variable and lets you work with arrays and dynamic memory efficiently.

The two operators

  • & (address-of): &x is the address where x lives.
  • * (dereference): if p holds the address of x, then *p is the value of x. Writing *p = 20; changes x itself.

Declare a pointer with * in the type: int *p = &x; means p points to an int.

Pointer arithmetic

Adding 1 to a pointer moves it by the size of what it points to. For an int pointer, p + 1 jumps 4 bytes to the next int — that is how array indexing works: arr[i] is the same as *(arr + i).

Danger: wild and NULL pointers

An uninitialised pointer points nowhere safe, and dereferencing NULL (address 0) crashes the program. Always initialise pointers, and check for NULL before dereferencing.

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int x = 10;
    int *p = &x;
    printf("x = %d\n", x);
    printf("address of x = %p\n", (void *)p);
    *p = 20;
    printf("x is now %d\n", x);
    return 0;
}

%p prints an address (the cast to void * is the correct, portable way to print a pointer). After *p = 20;, x itself is 20 because p points at x.

Key points

  • A pointer stores a memory address; int *p = &x; makes p point to x.
  • &x gives the address of x; *p gives the value at the address p holds.
  • *p = 20; changes the variable p points to.
  • p + 1 moves to the next element, not the next byte.
  • Never dereference an uninitialised or NULL pointer — it crashes.

flowchart.title: How a pointer changes a variable

mcqs.q: int x = 10; int *p = &x; What is *p?
mcqs.why: p holds the address of x, so dereferencing it with * gives the value stored at that address, which is 10.

mcqs.q: What does &x mean in C?
mcqs.why: & is the address-of operator; &x is the memory address where x is stored.

mcqs.q: int *p points to an int. How many bytes does p + 1 move forward (typical 4-byte int)?
mcqs.why: Pointer arithmetic steps by the size of the pointed-to type, so an int pointer advances by sizeof(int), typically 4 bytes.

mcqs.q: What happens if you dereference a NULL pointer?
mcqs.why: NULL is address 0, which the program does not own; dereferencing it causes a segmentation fault and the program crashes.

mcqs.q: After int x = 10; int *p = &x; *p = 20; what is x?
mcqs.why: *p = 20 writes 20 into the memory p points to, which is x itself, so x becomes 20.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: *p is x, so *p = *p + 3 reads 5, adds 3 and writes 8 back into x.
tasks.hint: *p is just another name for x here. What is 5 + 3?

tasks.title: Fix the pointer declaration
tasks.prompt: This program will not compile. Fix it so p points to a.
tasks.answer: p was declared as a plain int, so it cannot hold an address and cannot be dereferenced. Declaring it as int *p makes it a pointer to int, so &a fits and *p reads 42.
tasks.hint: p must be declared as a pointer type, not a plain int.

tasks.title: Trace the pointer swap
tasks.prompt: Trace this swap step by step.
tasks.answer: p points to a and q points to b. temp saves *p (3), *p = *q writes 7 into a, and *q = temp writes 3 into b. The values are swapped through the pointers.
tasks.hint: Follow each dereference: *p means a, *q means b.

lessons.title: Structures & File Handling
lessons.body:
Structures: group related data

A structure groups different types under one name. A student has a name (string), a roll number (int) and marks (float) — one struct holds them all together instead of three separate arrays.

struct Student {
    char name[50];
    int roll;
    float marks;
};

Access members with the dot operator: struct Student s1; s1.roll = 101;. An array of structs, struct Student class[30];, holds a whole class.

Files: data that survives

Variables vanish when a program ends; files keep data. Open a file with fopen, which returns a FILE *, use it, then close it with fclose.

  • "r" — read an existing file (fails if it does not exist)
  • "w" — write, creating the file or erasing its old contents
  • "a" — append to the end without erasing

Always check the result: if fopen returns NULL, the file could not be opened. Use fprintf to write formatted text and fscanf to read it back.

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    struct Student {
        char name[50];
        int roll;
        float marks;
    };
    struct Student s1 = {"Sid", 101, 88.5f};
    FILE *fp = fopen("students.txt", "w");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        printf("Could not open file\n");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(fp, "%s %d %.1f\n", s1.name, s1.roll, s1.marks);
    fclose(fp);
    printf("Saved %s\n", s1.name);
    return 0;
}

Forgetting fclose can lose the last buffered data, so always close files you open. Note the f suffix: 88.5f is a float literal; without it the value is a double.

Key points

  • A struct groups different types into one named unit; members are accessed with .
  • An array of structs stores a whole collection, like a class of students.
  • fopen modes: "r" read, "w" write (erases), "a" append.
  • Always check fopen for NULL before using the file.
  • Always fclose a file you opened, or buffered data can be lost.

flowchart.title: How a file is saved safely

mcqs.q: How do you access the roll member of struct Student s1?
mcqs.why: The dot operator accesses a member of a struct variable; -> is only for pointers to structs.

mcqs.q: What does fopen("data.txt", "w") do if data.txt already exists?
options: Erases its contents and starts fresh
mcqs.why: "w" mode truncates an existing file to zero length before writing; "a" is the mode that appends.

mcqs.q: What does fopen return when it cannot open the file?
mcqs.why: On failure fopen returns NULL, which is why programs must check the result before using the FILE pointer.

mcqs.q: Why must you call fclose() on a file you opened?
options: It is optional and does nothing
To flush buffered data and free the file
mcqs.why: fclose flushes any data still in the output buffer to disk and releases the file handle; skipping it can lose data.

mcqs.q: Which mode opens a file for reading?
mcqs.why: "r" is read mode; "w" writes (erasing) and "a" appends.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.answer: p.x is 3 and p.y is 4 from the initialiser {3, 4}, printed in order.
tasks.hint: The initialiser fills members in order: x first, then y.

tasks.title: Fix the file handling bug
tasks.prompt: This program can lose data and crash on a missing folder. Fix both problems.
tasks.answer: Two bugs: fopen can return NULL (e.g. bad path), and fprintf on NULL crashes, so a NULL check is added. And the file was never closed, so buffered data could be lost — fclose flushes it to disk.
tasks.hint: Two fixes: check what fopen returned, and close the file when done.

tasks.title: Fill in the blanks
tasks.prompt: Complete the program so it writes a student's name to a file.
tasks.expected:
w
fclose
tasks.answer: "w" opens the file for writing, and fclose(fp) flushes and closes it.
tasks.hint: First blank: the write mode letter. Second blank: the function that closes a file.

lessons.title: Recursion & Problem Solving
lessons.body:
What is recursion?

Recursion is when a function calls itself. A problem is split into a smaller copy of itself until it becomes so small it can be answered directly. Factorial is the classic example: n! = n * (n-1)!.

The two parts every recursive function needs

  • Base case — the stopping condition. For factorial, 0! = 1. Without it the function calls itself forever and crashes with a stack overflow.
  • Recursive step — the call on a smaller input, moving towards the base case.

How it runs

Each call waits on the call stack while the next call runs. factorial(3) calls factorial(2), which calls factorial(1), which calls factorial(0) — the base case returns 1, then the answers unwind: 1 * 1 = 1, 2 * 1 = 2, 3 * 2 = 6.

#include <stdio.h>

int factorial(int n)
{
    if (n == 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

int main(void)
{
    printf("5! = %d\n", factorial(5));
    return 0;
}

Recursion is elegant for problems that break into smaller copies — factorial, Fibonacci, searching trees — but a loop is usually faster and safer for simple counting, because each recursive call uses stack memory.

Key points

  • Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller input.
  • Every recursive function needs a base case, or it recurses forever and overflows the stack.
  • The recursive step must move towards the base case.
  • factorial(5) = 120 and factorial(0) = 1.
  • Prefer loops for simple counting; use recursion when the problem naturally splits into smaller copies.

mcqs.q: What is factorial(4)?
What is factorial(0)?
mcqs.why: By definition 0! = 1, and it is also the base case that stops the recursion.

mcqs.q: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
options: It calls itself forever and overflows the stack
mcqs.why: Without a stopping condition the calls never end; each call uses stack memory until the stack overflows and the program crashes.

mcqs.q: What does the recursive step of factorial do?
mcqs.why: The recursive step reduces the problem: n! = n * (n-1)!, so it calls factorial(n - 1).

mcqs.q: Which problem is recursion naturally suited to?
options: Reading a file line by line
mcqs.why: Factorial and Fibonacci break into smaller copies of themselves, which is exactly what recursion expresses; simple counting is better as a loop.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.hint: 5! means 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1.

tasks.title: Fix the missing base case
tasks.prompt: This recursive function never stops. Fix it.
tasks.answer: There is no base case, so countdown keeps calling itself with ever-smaller n until the stack overflows. Adding if (n == 0) return 0; stops the recursion after printing 3 2 1.
tasks.hint: Every recursive function needs a condition that stops the calls.

tasks.title: Trace factorial(3)
tasks.prompt: Trace factorial(3) step by step using the lesson flowchart.
tasks.expected: factorial(3): n!=0, returns 3*factorial(2); factorial(2) returns 2*factorial(1); factorial(1) returns 1*factorial(0); factorial(0) returns 1; unwinds: 1*1=1, 2*1=2, 3*2=6.
tasks.answer: Following the flowchart: 3 is not 0, so it calls factorial(2); 2 is not 0, so it calls factorial(1); 1 is not 0, so it calls factorial(0); 0 hits the Yes edge and returns 1. The pending multiplications then unwind: 1*1=1, 2*1=2, 3*2=6.
tasks.hint: Walk down to the base case, then multiply back up.

lessons.title: Mini Project: Student Marks Manager
lessons.body:
The project

Now combine everything: build a Student Marks Manager that stores up to 5 students, each with a name, roll number and marks in 3 subjects. It must show a menu, add students, display all students with totals and averages, find the topper, and save the records to a file.

Step 1: Model the data

Use a struct for one student and an array of structs for the class — the same pattern from Lesson 8. Keep a count of how many students have been added so far.

Step 2: The menu loop

A do-while loop shows the menu at least once and repeats until the user chooses Exit. Each choice calls a small function: addStudent, displayAll, findTopper, saveToFile.

Step 3: Totals and averages

Total is the sum of the 3 subject marks; average is total / 3.0 — remember the integer division trap from Lesson 3, so divide by 3.0, not 3. The topper is the student with the highest total: scan the array keeping the best total seen so far.

Step 4: Save to a file

Open students.txt in "w" mode, check for NULL, write one line per student with fprintf, then fclose.

#include <stdio.h>

struct Student {
    char name[50];
    int roll;
    int marks[3];
};

int totalMarks(struct Student s)
{
    return s.marks[0] + s.marks[1] + s.marks[2];
}

int main(void)
{
    struct Student s1 = {"Sid", 101, {78, 85, 90}};
    int total = totalMarks(s1);
    printf("%s total: %d, average: %.1f\n",
           s1.name, total, total / 3.0);
    return 0;
}

Output: Sid total: 253, average: 84.3. This is the core calculation your full menu program will reuse for every student.

Key points

  • Model one student as a struct and the class as an array of structs.
  • A do-while menu loop runs until the user chooses Exit.
  • Average is total / 3.0 — dividing by 3 would truncate the result.
  • Find the topper by scanning for the highest total.
  • Save records with fopen in "w" mode, check for NULL, and fclose.

flowchart.title: How the Marks Manager menu works

video.title: C Programming Full Course for free ⚙️

mcqs.q: Which data structure best stores 5 students, each with a name, roll and marks?
mcqs.why: An array of structs groups each student's mixed fields together and holds all 5 in one collection.

mcqs.q: A student scored 78, 85 and 90. What is the correct average in C?
mcqs.why: 253 / 3 is integer division and gives 84; 253 / 3.0 forces floating-point division and gives 84.333..., printed as 84.3.

mcqs.q: Which loop is best for a menu that must show at least once?
mcqs.why: do-while checks its condition after the body, so the menu is guaranteed to display at least once.

mcqs.q: Which fopen mode saves the student records to a file?
mcqs.why: "w" opens the file for writing, creating it if needed, so the records can be saved.

mcqs.q: How do you find the topper among the students?
options: Scan all students and keep the highest total
mcqs.why: The topper is the student with the highest total marks, found by scanning every student and tracking the best total seen so far.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this program print?
tasks.hint: Add the three marks, then divide by 3.0 for a real average.

tasks.title: Fix the truncated average
tasks.prompt: This program prints the average as 84 instead of 84.3. Fix it.
tasks.answer: total / 3 is integer division: 253 / 3 = 84 with the fraction discarded, and %.1f then prints 84.0. Dividing by 3.0 forces floating-point division, giving 84.333... which %.1f prints as 84.3.
tasks.hint: The division itself is the problem, not the format specifier.

tasks.title: Trace the topper search
tasks.prompt: Trace the search for the topper among totals 253, 240 and 271.
tasks.expected: i=0: 253>0, best=253, topper=0; i=1: 240>253 false; i=2: 271>253, best=271, topper=2; topper index 2.
tasks.answer: Start with best 0. i=0: 253 beats 0, so best=253, topper=0. i=1: 240 does not beat 253, no change. i=2: 271 beats 253, so best=271, topper=2. The topper is the student at index 2.
tasks.hint: Walk the loop: only update best and topper when the total beats the current best.

tasks.title: Build the Student Marks Manager
tasks.prompt: Build the full Student Marks Manager in C: a menu program (do-while loop) that stores up to 5 students (name, roll number, marks in 3 subjects) in an array of structs, and offers: 1. Add student, 2. Display all students with total and average, 3. Show topper, 4. Save all records to students.txt, 5. Exit. Validate input (marks 0-100, no more than 5 students) and handle fopen failure.
tasks.expected: Program compiles with gcc without warnings; menu repeats until Exit; adding a 6th student is refused; totals and averages are correct (average uses / 3.0); topper is the highest total; students.txt contains one line per student; file errors are handled with a message.
tasks.answer: Approach: define struct Student with name, roll and marks[3]; keep a count variable. Write small functions: addStudent, displayAll, findTopper, saveToFile, plus totalMarks. Drive them from a do-while menu with a switch. Reuse the lesson code for totals, averages and file saving, and test with the sample student Sid (78, 85, 90).
tasks.hint: Build it in small pieces: struct first, then add/display, then topper, then file saving.
